questiontext.text: A program slice is best described as:

answer.text: The set of statements that can affect (or be affected by) the value of a chosen variable at a chosen point

feedback.text: Correct — a slice keeps only the statements relevant to a variable at a program point.

answer.text: The set of all statements that a test suite executes at least once

feedback.text: That is executed/covered code, not a slice; a slice is defined by dependence on a variable at a point.

answer.text: A contiguous block of source lines between two line numbers

feedback.text: A slice need not be contiguous; it is any subset of statements linked by dependences to the criterion.

answer.text: The list of variables that a function declares

feedback.text: A slice is a set of statements, not a set of variable declarations.

generalfeedback.text: A slice is the subset of a program's statements that influence, or are influenced by, a variable at a specific location — computed via control and data dependences.

questiontext.text: In the explorer, a slicing criterion is specified as which pair?

answer.text: A statement (program point) together with a variable

feedback.text: Correct — the criterion is ⟨statement, variable⟩; you pick a statement and then one of its variables.

answer.text: A test input together with an expected output

feedback.text: That describes a test case, not a slicing criterion.

answer.text: A start line together with an end line

feedback.text: A criterion is a point and a variable, not a line range.

answer.text: A function name together with its return type

feedback.text: The criterion targets a variable at a statement, not a function signature.

generalfeedback.text: A slicing criterion is a pair ⟨statement s, variable v⟩. The explorer builds it when you click a statement and then choose one of its variables.

questiontext.text: For criterion ⟨s, v⟩, the backward slice contains the statements that:

answer.text: May affect the value of v at s

feedback.text: Correct — a backward slice gathers everything that could influence v at s.

answer.text: May be affected by the value of v at s

feedback.text: That is the forward slice, the opposite direction.

answer.text: Are executed after s in every run

feedback.text: Position in the run does not define the backward slice; dependence on v does.

answer.text: Assign a constant to v

feedback.text: The backward slice is not restricted to constant assignments; it is any statement transitively influencing v at s.

generalfeedback.text: The backward slice on ⟨s, v⟩ is the set of statements that may affect the value of v at s, following control and data dependences backwards.

questiontext.text: For criterion ⟨s, v⟩, the forward slice contains the statements that:

answer.text: May be affected by the value of v at s

feedback.text: Correct — a forward slice gathers everything that the value of v at s could influence.

answer.text: May affect the value of v at s

feedback.text: That is the backward slice, the opposite direction.

answer.text: Are executed before s in every run

feedback.text: The forward slice is about being influenced by v, not about textual or temporal position.

answer.text: Read v but never define any variable

feedback.text: Forward-slice statements can define variables; they are simply reachable from v at s via dependences.

generalfeedback.text: The forward slice on ⟨s, v⟩ is the set of statements that may be affected by the value of v at s, following dependences forward.

questiontext.text: What distinguishes a dynamic slice from a static slice?

answer.text: A dynamic slice is computed for one specific execution (a given input/trace); a static slice holds for all possible executions

feedback.text: Correct — the dynamic slice is restricted to the statements and dependences actually exercised by a chosen run.

answer.text: A dynamic slice uses only data dependences; a static slice uses only control dependences

feedback.text: Both kinds use control and data dependences; the difference is per-run versus all-runs.

answer.text: A dynamic slice is always the forward slice; a static slice is always the backward slice

feedback.text: Direction (forward/backward) is independent of static/dynamic.

answer.text: A dynamic slice ignores the criterion; a static slice needs one

feedback.text: Both need a criterion; the dynamic slice adds a specific execution.

generalfeedback.text: A static slice is valid for every possible run; a dynamic slice is specialised to one execution (a specific input/trace), so it keeps only the dependences that were actually live in that run.

questiontext.text: There is a data dependence from statement A to statement B when:

answer.text: A defines a variable that B later uses, with no redefinition in between

feedback.text: Correct — a def in A reaches a use in B (a def-use relationship).

answer.text: A and B appear on consecutive source lines

feedback.text: Adjacency is irrelevant; a data dependence is a reaching def-use link.

answer.text: A decides whether B executes

feedback.text: That is a control dependence, not a data dependence.

answer.text: A and B call the same function

feedback.text: Sharing a callee is not what creates a data dependence.

generalfeedback.text: A data dependence A → B (on variable v) means A defines v and B uses that value of v — a def reaching a use.

questiontext.text: There is a control dependence from statement A to statement B when:

answer.text: Whether B executes depends on the outcome of a predicate at A (e.g. an if or loop condition)

feedback.text: Correct — A is a branch/loop predicate that governs whether B runs.

answer.text: A defines a variable that B reads

feedback.text: That is a data dependence, not a control dependence.

answer.text: A and B are in the same function

feedback.text: Being co-located in a function does not create a control dependence.

answer.text: B always executes immediately after A

feedback.text: Sequential order alone is not control dependence; a governing predicate is required.

generalfeedback.text: A control dependence A → B means A is a predicate (branch or loop condition) whose outcome decides whether B is executed.

questiontext.text: The program dependence graph (PDG) drawn by the explorer has nodes and edges standing for:

answer.text: Nodes are statements; edges are control and data dependences

feedback.text: Correct — the PDG links statements by their control and data dependences.

answer.text: Nodes are variables; edges are assignments

feedback.text: PDG nodes are statements, not variables.

answer.text: Nodes are functions; edges are calls

feedback.text: That describes a call graph, not a PDG.

answer.text: Nodes are basic blocks; edges are the sequential flow of control only

feedback.text: That is closer to a control-flow graph; a PDG carries both control and data dependence edges over statements.

generalfeedback.text: In a PDG each node is a statement and each edge is a control or data dependence. Slicing is graph reachability over these edges from the criterion.

questiontext.text: Every slice computed by the explorer always contains the criterion statement itself.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the slice is seeded with the criterion statement, so it is always a member.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The slice always includes the criterion statement; the algorithm seeds the result set with it.

generalfeedback.text: Both backward and forward slices start from the criterion statement and add dependent statements, so the criterion statement is always in the slice.

name.text: Read the slice: grade on return

questiontext.text:
In the Grade Average example:

2:  total = 0
3:  count = 0
4:  for (const s of scores)
5:    total = total + s
6:    count = count + 1
8:  avg = total / count
9:  grade = avg >= 60 ? "pass" : "fail"
10: return grade

What is the backward slice for criterion ⟨line 10, grade⟩?

answer.text: All eight statements (lines 2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10)

feedback.text: Correct — grade depends on avg, which depends on both total and count, which depend on the loop and the initialisations, so the whole function is in the slice.

answer.text: Only line 10

feedback.text: The return uses grade, which transitively depends on almost every other statement, so the slice is far larger.

answer.text: Only lines 9 and 10

feedback.text: grade (line 9) depends on avg, which pulls in total and count and their loop — the slice is the whole function.

answer.text: Only lines 8, 9, 10

feedback.text: avg depends on total and count, dragging in lines 2–6 as well; the slice is all eight statements.

generalfeedback.text: Backward from grade: 10 ← 9 (grade) ← 8 (avg) ← 5,6 (total,count) ← 4 (loop), 2, 3. Every statement is reached, so the slice is the whole function.

name.text: Classify: sign excluded from label slice

questiontext.text: In the Classify example, the backward slice for criterion ⟨return label, label⟩ excludes every statement that assigns sign.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — sign never influences label, so the sign assignments (lines 3, 6, 9) are not in the slice.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The sign assignments do not affect label at all, so slicing on label drops them — a classic illustration of slicing's focus.

generalfeedback.text: label depends only on the label assignments and the predicates that guard them; the parallel sign computations are irrelevant and fall outside the slice.

name.text: Read the app: the loop node kind

questiontext.text: In the Grade Average example, line 4 for (const s of scores) appears in the PDG as which kind of node?

answer.text: A control (predicate) node that governs whether the loop body runs

feedback.text: Correct — the loop header is a control node; lines 5 and 6 are control-dependent on it.

answer.text: An output node

feedback.text: The output node is the return statement, not the loop header.

answer.text: A pure data node with no outgoing control edges

feedback.text: The loop header has control edges to the body statements it guards.

answer.text: A comment that is ignored by the slicer

feedback.text: The loop header is an executable control statement, not a comment.

generalfeedback.text: The loop header is a control node: statements in the loop body (lines 5 and 6) are control-dependent on it.

questiontext.text: Which pairing of direction and meaning is correct?

answer.text: Backward = "what may affect v"; Forward = "what v may affect"

feedback.text: Correct — backward looks at influences on v, forward at what v influences.

answer.text: Backward = "what v may affect"; Forward = "what may affect v"

feedback.text: These are swapped: backward is influences on v, forward is what v affects.

answer.text: Backward = earlier lines only; Forward = later lines only

feedback.text: Slices are defined by dependence, not by textual line order.

answer.text: Backward = data only; Forward = control only

feedback.text: Both directions follow control and data dependences.

generalfeedback.text: Backward slice = statements that may affect v at s; forward slice = statements that may be affected by v at s.

name.text: Dynamic slice never larger than static

questiontext.text: For the same criterion and program, a dynamic slice (for one run) is never larger than the corresponding static slice.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the dynamic slice is restricted to executed statements and live dependences, so it is a subset of the static slice.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Restricting to one run can only drop statements, never add them, so a dynamic slice is at most the size of the static slice.

generalfeedback.text: A dynamic slice keeps only the statements and dependence edges actually exercised in the chosen run, so it is a subset of (and at most as large as) the static slice.

questiontext.text: A primary practical benefit of program slicing is that it:

answer.text: Narrows attention to only the statements relevant to a variable at a point, aiding debugging and comprehension

feedback.text: Correct — a slice removes irrelevant code so you can focus on what can influence a suspect value.

answer.text: Guarantees the program is free of defects

feedback.text: Slicing isolates relevant code; it does not prove correctness.

answer.text: Automatically fixes the faulty statement

feedback.text: Slicing highlights relevant statements; it does not repair them.

answer.text: Increases the program's runtime performance

feedback.text: Slicing is an analysis aid, not a performance optimisation of the shipped program.

generalfeedback.text: Slicing reduces the code a developer must consider to the statements that can influence (or be influenced by) a variable at a point — valuable for debugging, understanding, and regression analysis.

questiontext.text:
Grade Average example:

2:  total = 0
3:  count = 0
4:  for (const s of scores)
5:    total = total + s
6:    count = count + 1
8:  avg = total / count
9:  grade = avg >= 60 ? "pass" : "fail"
10: return grade

What is the backward slice for criterion ⟨line 8, total⟩?

answer.text: Lines 2, 4, 5, 8

feedback.text: Correct — total at line 8 comes from line 5 (total+s), which is in the loop (line 4) and uses total from line 2.

answer.text: Lines 3, 4, 6, 8

feedback.text: Those are the count-related statements; the criterion variable is total, not count.

answer.text: All eight statements

feedback.text: Slicing on total at line 8 excludes the count computations (3, 6) and everything after line 8.

answer.text: Lines 5, 8 only

feedback.text: Line 5 depends on the loop (4) and the initial total (2), so those belong too.

generalfeedback.text: Backward from total at 8: 8 ← 5 (total = total+s) ← 4 (loop) and ← 2 (total = 0). count statements (3, 6) do not affect total, so they are excluded. Slice = {2, 4, 5, 8}.

questiontext.text: Using the same Grade Average program, what is the backward slice for criterion ⟨line 8, count⟩?

answer.text: Lines 3, 4, 6, 8

feedback.text: Correct — count at line 8 comes from line 6 (count+1), in the loop (line 4), initialised at line 3.

answer.text: Lines 2, 4, 5, 8

feedback.text: Those are the total-related statements; here the variable is count.

answer.text: Lines 3, 6, 8

feedback.text: Line 6 is control-dependent on the loop header (line 4), so line 4 belongs in the slice too.

answer.text: All eight statements

feedback.text: The total computations (2, 5) and the statements after line 8 do not affect count at line 8.

generalfeedback.text: Backward from count at 8: 8 ← 6 (count = count+1) ← 4 (loop) and ← 3 (count = 0). Slice = {3, 4, 6, 8}.

name.text: Why count is excluded from the total slice

questiontext.text: In the backward slice ⟨line 8, total⟩ of Grade Average, line 3 count = 0 is not included. Why?

answer.text: No dependence chain from count reaches total, so count cannot affect total's value at line 8

feedback.text: Correct — total and count are computed independently; count never flows into total.

answer.text: Because line 3 executes before the loop

feedback.text: Textual position is irrelevant; line 2 also runs before the loop yet is included. It is the absence of a dependence that excludes line 3.

answer.text: Because line 3 is a control statement

feedback.text: Line 3 is a plain assignment, not a control node; it is excluded because it does not affect total.

answer.text: Because count is used only after line 8

feedback.text: count is used at line 8 (in avg), but on the count operand, not on total; there is simply no total-dependence on count.

generalfeedback.text: A backward slice keeps only statements connected to the criterion variable by dependence edges. count is computed in a separate chain and never reaches total, so its initialisation is excluded.

questiontext.text: Grade Average example (lines as before). What is the forward slice for criterion ⟨line 2, total⟩?

feedback.text: Correct — total (line 2) flows into line 5, then into avg (8), grade (9), and the return (10).

answer.text: Lines 2, 3, 5, 6

feedback.text: Forward slicing follows where total's value goes; it does not pull in the count statements (3, 6).

answer.text: All eight statements

feedback.text: The initialisation line 3 and loop line 4 are upstream of, not affected by, total at line 2.

answer.text: Lines 2, 5 only

feedback.text: total reaches avg (8) via line 5, and avg then reaches grade (9) and the return (10).

generalfeedback.text: Forward from total at 2: 2 → 5 (total = total+s) → 8 (avg) → 9 (grade) → 10 (return). Slice = {2, 5, 8, 9, 10}.

questiontext.text:
Classify example:

2:  label = "zero"
3:  sign = 0
4:  if (n > 0)
5:    label = "positive"
6:    sign = 1
7:  else if (n < 0)
8:    label = "negative"
9:    sign = -1
11: return label

What is the backward slice for criterion ⟨line 11, label⟩?

feedback.text: Correct — label comes from the three label assignments (2, 5, 8) plus the predicates (4, 7) that guard 5 and 8.

answer.text: All nine statements

feedback.text: The sign assignments (3, 6, 9) never affect label and are excluded.
Lines 5 and 8 are control-dependent on the predicates 4 and 7, which must be in the slice too.

answer.text: Lines 5, 8, 11

feedback.text: The unconditional default label = "zero" (line 2) also reaches the return, and the guarding predicates belong too.

generalfeedback.text: label at 11 has reaching defs 2, 5, 8. Lines 5 and 8 are control-dependent on predicates 4 and 7. The sign statements (3, 6, 9) never influence label. Slice = {2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 11}.

name.text: Why sign is excluded from label slice

questiontext.text: In the Classify backward slice ⟨line 11, label⟩, line 6 sign = 1 is excluded. The best reason is:

answer.text: sign is never used to compute label, so no data dependence carries it into the return

feedback.text: Correct — label and sign are independent; sign has no path to label.

answer.text: sign = 1 is inside an if-branch, and slicing ignores branch bodies

feedback.text: Slicing does include branch bodies (line 5 is included); line 6 is dropped only because it does not affect label.

answer.text: sign = 1 executes only when n > 0, and the slice ignores conditional runs

feedback.text: Static slicing does not ignore conditional statements; line 6 is excluded for lack of dependence on label.

answer.text: sign is a constant, and constants are never sliced

feedback.text: Constant assignments can appear in slices (line 2 is one); the reason is that sign does not reach label.

generalfeedback.text: Slicing on label keeps only statements that reach label through dependences. sign is computed on a parallel, independent chain, so all sign assignments are excluded.

name.text: Why the loop header enters the slice

questiontext.text: In Grade Average, the backward slice ⟨line 5, total⟩ = {2, 4, 5}. Why is line 4 for (const s of scores) included, even though it does not assign total?

answer.text: Line 5 is control-dependent on the loop header, so the header must be in the slice

feedback.text: Correct — whether line 5 runs depends on the loop predicate at line 4, a control dependence.

answer.text: The loop header assigns total

feedback.text: The header defines the loop variable s, not total; it enters via control dependence.

answer.text: Line 4 is textually adjacent to line 5

feedback.text: Adjacency does not force inclusion; the control dependence does.

answer.text: Every slice always includes line 4

feedback.text: Line 4 is included only when a sliced statement is control-dependent on it, not unconditionally.

generalfeedback.text: Line 5 runs only when the loop iterates, so it is control-dependent on the loop header (line 4). Control dependences are followed in slicing, pulling line 4 in.

questiontext.text: Which explorer relationship is captured by a data-dependence edge?

answer.text: total = 0 (line 2) → total = total + s (line 5): a value defined then used

feedback.text: Correct — line 2 defines total, line 5 uses it; that is a def-use (data) dependence.

answer.text: for (line 4) → total = total + s (line 5): the loop deciding the body runs

feedback.text: That is a control dependence, not a data dependence.

answer.text: if (n > 0) (line 4) → label = "positive" (line 5) in Classify

feedback.text: That predicate-to-guarded-body link is a control dependence.

answer.text: return grade being the last line of the function

feedback.text: Being last is a positional fact, not a dependence edge.

generalfeedback.text: A data-dependence edge links a definition of a variable to a later use of that value. total defined at line 2 and used at line 5 is a data dependence.

questiontext.text: Which explorer relationship is captured by a control-dependence edge?

answer.text: if (n > 0) (line 4) → label = "positive" (line 5): the predicate governs whether the statement runs

feedback.text: Correct — line 5 executes only if the predicate at line 4 is true; that is a control dependence.

answer.text: total = total + s (line 5) → avg = total / count (line 8): a value flowing forward

feedback.text: That is a data dependence on total, not control.

answer.text: count = 0 (line 3) → count = count + 1 (line 6): a definition reused

feedback.text: That is a data dependence on count, not control.

answer.text: avg = total / count (line 8) → grade = ... (line 9): avg used to compute grade

feedback.text: That is a data dependence on avg, not control.

generalfeedback.text: A control-dependence edge links a predicate to the statements whose execution it governs. if (n > 0) governing label = "positive" is such an edge.

questiontext.text: Grade Average example. What is the backward slice for criterion ⟨line 5, total⟩ (the accumulation statement)?

answer.text: Lines 2, 4, 5

feedback.text: Correct — total at line 5 uses total from line 2 and is control-dependent on the loop header at line 4.

answer.text: Lines 2, 5

feedback.text: Line 5 is control-dependent on the loop header (line 4), which must be included.

answer.text: Lines 2, 4, 5, 8

feedback.text: Line 8 uses total but is downstream (forward), not something line 5 depends on.

answer.text: Line 5 only

feedback.text: total at line 5 depends on its initial value (line 2) and on the loop header (line 4).

generalfeedback.text: Backward from total at 5: it uses total (defined at line 2) and is control-dependent on the loop header (line 4). Slice = {2, 4, 5}.

questiontext.text: Classify example. What is the forward slice for criterion ⟨line 2, label⟩ (the default assignment)?

answer.text: Lines 2 and 11

feedback.text: Correct — the value assigned at line 2 can reach only the return that uses label (line 11).
Lines 5 and 8 redefine label independently; they are not affected by the value written at line 2.

answer.text: All nine statements

feedback.text: The value from line 2 flows only to the return; it does not reach the sign statements or the predicates.

answer.text: Line 2 only

feedback.text: label defined at line 2 is used at the return (line 11), so line 11 is in the forward slice.

generalfeedback.text: Forward from label at 2: the only use of that value is the return (line 11). Slice = {2, 11}.

name.text: Why return is not in a backward slice on avg

questiontext.text: In Grade Average, the backward slice ⟨line 9, avg⟩ = {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9} — it does not contain line 10 return grade. Why?

answer.text: The return depends on line 9, not the other way round; a backward slice keeps only statements that affect the criterion

feedback.text: Correct — line 10 is downstream of line 9, so it would appear in a forward slice, not this backward one.

answer.text: The return has no variables, so it is never sliced

feedback.text: The return uses grade and can appear in slices; it is excluded here only because it does not affect avg at line 9.

answer.text: Line 10 is unreachable

feedback.text: The return is reachable; it is simply downstream of the criterion.

answer.text: Backward slices never include the last statement

feedback.text: There is no such rule; the last statement can be in a backward slice if it affects the criterion.

generalfeedback.text: A backward slice gathers statements that affect the criterion. The return is affected by (comes after) line 9, so it belongs to the forward slice, not the backward one.

name.text: Why avg enters the grade slice

questiontext.text: In Grade Average, the backward slice ⟨line 10, grade⟩ includes line 8 avg = total / count. Which chain explains this?

answer.text: return uses grade; grade (line 9) uses avg; avg is defined at line 8 — a data-dependence chain

feedback.text: Correct — grade ← avg follows the def-use chain back to line 8.

answer.text: Line 8 is control-dependent on the return

feedback.text: There is no control dependence from the return to line 8; the link is data dependence via grade and avg.

answer.text: Line 8 and line 10 are on the same execution path, which is enough

feedback.text: Sharing a path is not sufficient; a dependence chain (grade ← avg) is what includes line 8.

answer.text: avg is a global variable

feedback.text: avg is a local; its inclusion is due to the data-dependence chain into grade.

generalfeedback.text: 10 uses grade → 9 defines grade from avg → 8 defines avg. Following these data dependences backward pulls line 8 into the slice.

questiontext.text: In the Classify example, line 6 sign = 1 belongs to the backward slice for criterion ⟨return label, label⟩.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — sign never affects label, so line 6 is not in the slice.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: sign is independent of label; the label slice is {2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 11} and excludes all sign assignments.

generalfeedback.text: The backward slice on label keeps only the label assignments and their guarding predicates; the sign computations (including line 6) are excluded.

questiontext.text: Grade Average example. What is the forward slice for criterion ⟨line 3, count⟩?

feedback.text: Correct — count (line 3) flows into line 6, then avg (8), grade (9), and the return (10).
That is the forward slice from total (line 2); here the variable is count.

answer.text: Lines 3, 6 only

feedback.text: count reaches avg at line 8, which then reaches grade (9) and the return (10).

answer.text: All eight statements

feedback.text: The total statements (2, 5) and the loop header are not affected by count's value at line 3.

generalfeedback.text: Forward from count at 3: 3 → 6 (count = count+1) → 8 (avg) → 9 (grade) → 10 (return). Slice = {3, 6, 8, 9, 10}.

questiontext.text: Classify example, run with input n = 5 (trace executes lines 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 11). What is the dynamic backward slice for criterion ⟨line 11, label⟩?

answer.text: Lines 4, 5, 11

feedback.text: Correct — on this run label at the return came from line 5 (guarded by line 4); the default line 2 was overwritten and never reaches the return.
That is the static slice; the dynamic slice for n = 5 is smaller because line 5 overwrote label, and lines 7, 8 did not execute.

answer.text: Lines 2, 5, 11

feedback.text: The default line 2 is dead on this run (label was reassigned at line 5); line 4 guards line 5 and is included instead.
The dynamic slice keeps only statements that actually influenced label — not every executed statement (lines 3 and 6 compute sign; line 2 was overwritten).

generalfeedback.text: On n = 5 the live definition of label reaching the return is line 5, control-dependent on line 4. Line 2's assignment is overwritten (dead), and lines 7, 8 never run. Dynamic slice = {4, 5, 11}.

name.text: Static vs dynamic slice size (Classify, n = 5)

questiontext.text: For Classify ⟨line 11, label⟩, the static backward slice has 6 statements while the dynamic slice for n = 5 has 3. What does this size difference chiefly reflect?

answer.text: The static slice must account for all inputs (all branches), while the one run took only one branch and made the other label definitions irrelevant

feedback.text: Correct — specialising to a single execution drops the untaken branches and dead definitions.

answer.text: The dynamic slice found extra dependences the static analysis missed

feedback.text: The dynamic slice is a subset; it cannot contain statements absent from the static slice.

answer.text: The static analysis was imprecise and over-approximated by mistake

feedback.text: The larger static slice is correct, not a mistake — it must be safe for every possible input.

answer.text: The two slices used different criteria

feedback.text: Both use the same criterion ⟨line 11, label⟩; only the scope (all runs vs one run) differs.

generalfeedback.text: The static slice covers every possible execution, so it includes all three label definitions and both predicates. The dynamic slice for n = 5 keeps only the statements that actually determined label on that run, hence it is smaller.

questiontext.text: Classify example, run with input n = 0 (trace executes lines 2, 3, 4, 7, 11). What is the dynamic backward slice for criterion ⟨line 11, label⟩?

answer.text: Lines 2, 11

feedback.text: Correct — neither branch reassigns label, so the returned label is the default from line 2; the predicates did not change it.
Lines 4 and 7 executed, but label = "zero" (line 2) is unconditional — it is not control-dependent on those predicates, so they are not in the dynamic slice.
That is the static slice; on n = 0 neither label reassignment (5, 8) executes.

answer.text: Line 11 only

feedback.text: The value returned came from line 2, so line 2 is in the slice.

generalfeedback.text: On n = 0 both branches are skipped, so label keeps its default from line 2. Line 2 is unconditional (not control-dependent on the predicates), so the executed predicates 4 and 7 stay out. Dynamic slice = {2, 11}.

questiontext.text: Classify example, run with input n = -3 (trace executes lines 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 11). What is the dynamic backward slice for criterion ⟨line 11, label⟩?

feedback.text: Correct — label came from line 8, which is control-dependent on line 7 (else-if), which is control-dependent on line 4.
Line 8 overwrote the default label; line 2's assignment is dead on this run and drops out.

answer.text: Lines 7, 8, 11

feedback.text: Line 7 is itself control-dependent on line 4 (it is only reached when n > 0 is false), so line 4 is included too.

answer.text: Lines 8, 11

feedback.text: Line 8 is guarded by predicate 7, which is guarded by predicate 4; both belong in the slice.

generalfeedback.text: On n = -3 the live def of label is line 8, control-dependent on line 7, which is control-dependent on line 4. Line 2 is overwritten. Dynamic slice = {4, 7, 8, 11}.

questiontext.text: In Grade Average, the static backward slice ⟨line 10, grade⟩ is all eight statements. For the run scores = [50] the dynamic slice is also all eight. Why is there no reduction here?

answer.text: Every statement executed and each one's value genuinely contributed to grade on that run, so nothing could be dropped

feedback.text: Correct — with no untaken branches or dead definitions relevant to grade, the dynamic slice equals the static one.

answer.text: Dynamic slices always equal static slices

feedback.text: Not in general — the Classify example shows strict reductions; here they happen to coincide.

answer.text: The run failed, and failing runs are not sliced

feedback.text: Runs are sliced regardless of outcome; the coincidence is due to every statement contributing.

answer.text: The criterion variable grade is global

feedback.text: grade is local; the equality comes from all statements genuinely influencing grade on this run.

generalfeedback.text: A dynamic slice shrinks when some statements did not execute or their definitions were killed before reaching the criterion. Here every statement ran and each fed into grade, so the dynamic slice matches the full static slice.

questiontext.text: Why can a dynamic slice never contain a statement that the static slice (same criterion) omits?

answer.text: The dynamic slice only restricts the static one to executed statements and live dependences; restriction can remove but never add statements

feedback.text: Correct — the dynamic slice is a filtered subset of the static slice.

answer.text: A dynamic slice uses more dependence edges than the static one

feedback.text: It uses fewer — only those live in the run — so it cannot exceed the static slice.

answer.text: Dynamic analysis discovers new statements at runtime

feedback.text: No new statements appear; the run selects among the program's existing statements.

answer.text: The static slice ignores control dependences

feedback.text: Static slicing uses control dependences too; the subset relation holds because the dynamic slice is a restriction.

generalfeedback.text: A dynamic slice keeps only the executed statements and the dependence edges that were live in the chosen run — a subset of what the static slice considers, so it is always contained in the static slice.

questiontext.text: The Grade Average (buggy) example changes line 6 to count = count + s (it adds the score instead of 1), so the average is wrong. For criterion ⟨line 10, grade⟩, how does the backward slice help debugging?

answer.text: The faulty line 6 is inside the backward slice of grade, so it is among the statements a developer must inspect for a wrong grade

feedback.text: Correct — count feeds avg feeds grade, so the buggy count update is in the slice for the wrong output.

answer.text: The slice excludes line 6, proving it cannot be the fault

feedback.text: On the contrary, line 6 is in the slice via count → avg → grade, so it is a suspect.

answer.text: The slice automatically rewrites line 6 to the correct code

feedback.text: Slicing narrows the suspects; it does not repair code.

answer.text: The slice proves the bug is in the return statement

feedback.text: The return merely propagates grade; slicing points to the whole influencing set, which includes the actual fault at line 6.

generalfeedback.text: Because count flows into avg and then grade, the buggy line 6 is inside the backward slice for grade. Slicing confines the search for a wrong grade to exactly the statements that could have caused it.

questiontext.text: In Grade Average, which chain of data dependences shows that line 2 total = 0 can influence the returned grade?

answer.text: 2 (total) → 5 (total) → 8 (avg) → 9 (grade) → 10 (return)

feedback.text: Correct — total flows into the accumulation, then avg, then grade, then the return.

answer.text: 2 (total) → 3 (count) → 8 (avg) → 10 (return)

feedback.text: total does not flow into count (line 3); the chain runs through line 5, not line 3.

answer.text: 2 (total) → 8 (avg) → 10 (return)

feedback.text: total reaches avg via the accumulation at line 5; the direct 2 → 8 edge does not exist, and grade (9) sits between avg and the return.

answer.text: 2 (total) → 4 (loop) → 9 (grade) → 10 (return)

feedback.text: Line 2 has no data edge into the loop header, and grade is computed from avg, not directly from the loop.

generalfeedback.text: Forward from total at line 2: total is used at line 5, whose result feeds avg (8), which feeds grade (9), which the return (10) uses. That is the data-dependence chain.

questiontext.text: Under the static slice-based regression criterion, after changing statement S, which tests must be re-run?

answer.text: Every test that executed at least one statement in the forward slice (impact set) of S

feedback.text: Correct — the forward slice of S bounds everything the edit can affect, so any test touching it must re-run.

answer.text: Only the single test with the highest coverage

feedback.text: Coverage magnitude is irrelevant; what matters is whether a test touches S's impact set.

answer.text: Only tests that executed S itself, never any downstream statement

feedback.text: A test can be affected by touching a statement downstream of S even if it did not execute S directly.

answer.text: Every test in the suite, unconditionally

feedback.text: Slice-based selection avoids re-running tests that cannot be affected by the change.

generalfeedback.text: The forward slice of the changed statement is its impact set. The static criterion re-runs any test that executed at least one statement in that set, and safely skips the rest.

questiontext.text: Why does slicing reduce the cost of regression testing?

answer.text: It bounds the effect of a change to the change's slice (impact set), so tests that cannot reach that set can be safely skipped

feedback.text: Correct — only tests touching the impact set need re-running, saving effort.

answer.text: It deletes the tests that previously failed

feedback.text: Slicing selects which tests to re-run; it does not delete tests.

answer.text: It makes each test execute faster

feedback.text: Slicing reduces the number of tests to run, not the speed of an individual test.

answer.text: It guarantees the change introduced no defects

feedback.text: Slicing helps choose tests; it cannot by itself guarantee correctness.

generalfeedback.text: A change can only affect statements in its (forward) slice. Tests that never execute any statement in that impact set cannot observe the change, so they need not be re-run.

name.text: Forward slice from a loop variable

questiontext.text: Grade Average example. What is the forward slice for criterion ⟨line 4, s⟩ (the loop variable)?

feedback.text: Correct — line 4 controls the body (lines 5, 6) and its variable s feeds line 5; the effect then propagates through avg, grade, and the return.
Line 6 is control-dependent on the loop header (line 4), so it belongs to the forward slice too.

answer.text: All eight statements

feedback.text: The initialisations at lines 2 and 3 precede the loop and are not affected by s at line 4.

answer.text: Lines 4, 5, 6

feedback.text: The loop body updates total and count, whose values then reach avg (8), grade (9), and the return (10).

generalfeedback.text: Forward from the loop header: it controls lines 5 and 6, and s feeds line 5. Their effects flow into avg (8), grade (9), and the return (10). Lines 2 and 3 are upstream and excluded. Slice = {4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10}.

name.text: Predicate in a slice via control dependence

questiontext.text: In Classify, the backward slice ⟨line 11, label⟩ contains line 4 if (n > 0), even though line 4 assigns no variable that label uses. What justifies its inclusion?

answer.text: Line 5 (label = "positive") is control-dependent on line 4, and line 5 is in the slice, so its controlling predicate is pulled in

feedback.text: Correct — control dependences are followed backward, so a predicate guarding a sliced statement is included.

answer.text: Line 4 defines n, which label uses

feedback.text: label does not use n, and line 4 does not define it; inclusion is by control dependence of line 5.

answer.text: Every if-statement is always added to every slice

feedback.text: A predicate is added only when it controls a statement already in the slice.

answer.text: Line 4 is the first executable line

feedback.text: Being early does not force inclusion; the control dependence of line 5 does.

generalfeedback.text: label = "positive" (line 5) is in the slice and is control-dependent on the predicate at line 4. Slicing follows that control edge, so the predicate joins the slice.

name.text: Why the default label drops out (n = 5)

questiontext.text: In the dynamic slice of Classify for n = 5 ⟨line 11, label⟩, line 2 label = "zero" executed but is not in the slice. Why?

answer.text: Line 5 redefined label after line 2, so by the last-definition rule the value reaching the return came from line 5, not line 2

feedback.text: Correct — line 2's write is killed by line 5 before the return uses label, so it is a dead definition on this run.

answer.text: Line 2 never executed on this run

feedback.text: Line 2 did execute; it is excluded because its value was overwritten, not because it was skipped.

answer.text: Constant assignments are always excluded from dynamic slices

feedback.text: Constant assignments can appear in slices (line 5 assigns a constant and is included); line 2 is dropped as a dead definition.

answer.text: label = "zero" is control-dependent on line 4

feedback.text: Line 2 is unconditional; it is excluded because its value did not reach the return, not by control dependence.

generalfeedback.text: By the last-definition rule, only the most recent def of a variable before a use is live. On n = 5, line 5 overwrote label before the return, so line 2's definition is dead and excluded from the dynamic slice.

name.text: Smallest dynamic slice among the runs

questiontext.text: For Classify ⟨line 11, label⟩, compare the dynamic slices for the three inputs. Which input yields the smallest dynamic slice?

answer.text: n = 0 (slice = {2, 11}, size 2)

feedback.text: Correct — with neither branch reassigning label, only the default and the return remain, the smallest slice.

answer.text: n = 5 (slice = {4, 5, 11}, size 3)

feedback.text: That is size 3; the n = 0 run gives a smaller slice of size 2.
That is size 4, the largest of the three dynamic slices.

answer.text: All three are the same size

feedback.text: They differ: sizes 2 (n = 0), 3 (n = 5), and 4 (n = -3).

generalfeedback.text: Dynamic slices: n = 0 → {2, 11} (2), n = 5 → {4, 5, 11} (3), n = -3 → {4, 7, 8, 11} (4). The n = 0 run is smallest because the returned label is just the unconditional default.

name.text: How slicing aids debugging in general

questiontext.text: Overall, how does program slicing most directly help debugging?

answer.text: It narrows the search for a fault to the statements that can influence the incorrect variable at the failure point

feedback.text: Correct — the backward slice of the faulty value bounds the set of statements to inspect.

answer.text: It reruns the program until the bug disappears

feedback.text: Slicing is a static/dynamic analysis of dependences, not a retry mechanism.

answer.text: It ranks statements by execution time

feedback.text: Slicing is about dependences, not profiling execution time.

answer.text: It formally verifies the absence of the fault

feedback.text: Slicing focuses attention; it does not prove correctness.

generalfeedback.text: When a variable holds a wrong value at some point, its backward slice contains exactly the statements that could have caused it, so the developer can ignore the rest of the program.
